profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at a mid-size medical device manufacturer developing a reusable home-use infusion controller with a disposable drug cartridge for biologic therapy. The team is reviewing an existing proposal for the final pre-freeze design package after recent regulatory updates pushed the company to better integrate design decisions with downstream validation. The agenda is to assess whether the revised cartridge-door design, user-interface materials, and planned pilot build are sufficiently mature for a validation-focused design freeze, and to decide what modifications are needed before conditional approval. The expected outcome is a go/no-go recommendation on the current package, plus a short list of actions to make the design more defensible for human-factors and regulatory validation.

members.name: Daniel Mercer
members.expertise: Electromechanical device architecture, design controls, verification planning, pilot-build readiness
members.background: Mechanical engineer with 12 years in infusion and drug-delivery devices, known for moving designs from prototype to manufacturable pilot builds under tight timelines.
members.private_state: He wants this review to end with a conditional approval so the April pilot-tooling slot is not lost, and he is quietly worried that validation-related requests will expand late and trigger another design iteration.
hidden_assumptions: A 'validation-ready build' can use line-like pilot units as long as the core device form, fit, and function are frozen; minor updates to IFU wording or packaging can happen afterward without undermining the study.
In a design review, 'labeling' mainly means the controlled text on the device, cartridge, and primary instructions for use, not every commercial or support-facing artifact.

When people say 'worst-case use,' they usually mean the harshest device operating conditions already covered by engineering verification, such as low battery, cold-soak startup, or repeated door cycles.
For this therapy, a brief nurse walkthrough at initiation is a standard part of real-world onboarding, so it is reasonable to assume users will have that baseline orientation.
If the hardware and software are frozen, the remaining validation discussion is mostly about documenting rationale rather than changing what the design package includes.

members.name: Dr. Priya Shah
members.role: Clinical and Human Factors Regulatory Lead
members.expertise: Human factors validation, clinical workflow analysis, EU MDR/FDA submission strategy, use-related risk documentation
members.background: Former infusion nurse who moved into regulatory affairs and has led human-factors packages for several home-use combination products.
members.private_state: She wants the package to be defensible in front of a notified body and human-factors reviewers, and she is concerned that engineering still treats validation as something that can be patched in after design freeze.
hidden_assumptions: A 'validation-ready build' must be production-equivalent from the user perspective, including packaging, quick-start materials, and the exact set of support materials patients will encounter.

In a home-use medical device context, 'labeling' includes every controlled user-facing support element that shapes safe use, such as carton cues, quick-start cards, reminder stickers, and scripted support content.
When people say 'worst-case use,' they usually mean the use situation most likely to provoke error, such as nighttime setup, first-time cartridge replacement, or responding to an alarm under stress.
Home-use validation should assume only standardized, documented onboarding materials; clinic-specific coaching is not automatically part of the validated user interface unless formally included.
If a design review says the package is ready, that implies the validation boundary has already been defined across device, documentation, and intended use context.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both members refer to the April units as the 'validation-ready build' or 'pilot build.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means line-like pilot units with frozen hardware/software and production-intent assembly, even if IFU wording, packaging details, or support artifacts are still being refined.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means production-equivalent units as experienced by the user, including finalized packaging and all user-facing materials that would be present during validation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In medical device work, both disciplines routinely use the phrase 'validation-ready' as if it were standard, and each assumes the other shares their discipline's implicit threshold for what must already be finalized.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that 'labeling updates' should be completed around the review package.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 treats labeling as the on-device graphics, cartridge markings, and formal IFU pages attached to the design file.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes the quick-start card, outer carton cues, reminder stickers, and helpline or support-facing content that users rely on during setup and troubleshooting.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The term 'labeling' sounds settled and regulatory, so neither person feels a need to enumerate artifacts; each assumes their own boundary is the ordinary one for this stage of review.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to cover 'worst-case use'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both members say the validation rationale should address 'worst-case use scenarios.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks coverage is adequate if the rationale references device-stress conditions already exercised in verification, such as cold-start operation, low battery, and repeated cartridge-door actuation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks coverage is adequate only if the rationale includes the use contexts most likely to generate errors, such as first-time nighttime cartridge changes after an occlusion alarm.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both framings sound safety-oriented and legitimate, so the phrase 'worst-case' creates false consensus even though they are applying different standards for what counts as a sufficiently challenging use case.

misalignment_points.topic: What users normally receive during onboarding
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to 'standard onboarding' or 'what users normally get at initiation.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes that a short nurse walkthrough at therapy initiation is an established part of normal use and therefore can be assumed when shaping validation plans.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes that only formally controlled and standardized onboarding materials count; informal clinic coaching is not part of the validated use environment unless explicitly built into the design package.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because therapy initiation often does involve some instruction in practice, it feels natural to speak as though 'standard onboarding' is shared knowledge, even though they silently disagree about whether that context is part of the controlled design under review.
